content.title: Group Content With Semantic Structure
content.hook: A real page often has recognizable regions:
content.context:
- the top area of the page
- navigation links
- the main content
- supporting content
- the bottom area

HTML gives us meaningful elements for many of these jobs.
goals: Use meaningful structural elements to group page regions and distinguish them from generic containers.

content.title: Meet the semantic containers
content.text:
For this lesson, learn these elements:

- `<header>` — introductory content for a page or section
- `<nav>` — a region containing navigation links
- `<main>` — the primary content of the page
- `<section>` — a grouped section of related content
- `<footer>` — closing or supporting information for a page or section

These elements do not exist just to make the page look different. They describe what each region is.

content.question: Where does a group of primary navigation links belong in this model?

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. `<main>`, `<section>`, and `<footer>` represent other page regions; HTML provides a dedicated landmark specifically for primary navigation links.

content.question: You have a page region containing the primary content of the page. Which element should you start with?

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. `<header>`, `<nav>`, and `<footer>` are for introductory, navigation, and closing content. Which landmark wraps the central content unique to this page?

content.question:
A page has one main content area. Inside it are two related groups: “Lessons” and “Projects.”

Which structure is the clearest starting model?

options.text: Two `<main>` elements with no surrounding relationship

feedback.correct: The page has one primary content area, and that area contains related sections.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A document has one primary `<main>` content area, and thematic groups inside that primary area are represented with `<section>` elements.

content.question:
A teammate says: “Semantic HTML is extra paperwork. A pile of generic containers can hold the same text.”

What is the strongest response?

options.text: Meaningful elements make the document’s structure clearer to humans and tools.
Semantic elements are only for colors.
Every page must use exactly five semantic elements.

feedback.correct: Semantic structure communicates relationships and purpose instead of hiding everything behind generic containers.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Generic `<div>` elements can hold text, and semantic HTML is not about colors or arbitrary tag counts—it communicates the purpose of each region to browsers, assistive technology, and developers.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** A page is made of meaningful regions, not just generic containers.
**Senior habit:** Prefer an element that communicates the region’s job before reaching for a generic container.
nextSteps: Complete the lesson activities and demonstrate the target skill without relying on unseen concepts from later modules.
